title.value: Questions Regarding LLM Baseline Choices and KernelBench Runtime Measurement

comment.value:
As several ICLR’26 submissions have noted, LLM-based CUDA kernel optimization is a rapidly evolving area, and KernelBench has become a common evaluation target. Across discussions in LU27DiW5ik, f4GtuI2blh, and related threads, multiple methodological concerns around KernelBench and LLM reasoning capability have been raised. These issues relate to evaluation design rather than agent architecture, yet they do not appear in this paper’s official reviews.

Two aspects of the evaluation setup may benefit from clarification:

1. **LLM choice and baseline completeness.**
The paper reports using Claude Sonnet 4 for both baselines and agents (lines 393–394, 657–658). Reviews such as LU27DiW5ik (note Mz8jC1vxt4) and c339hUw3cy (note frQ14SVqTX) argue that comparisons with lower-cost LLMs are important for understanding generality. From a CUDA/HPC evaluation perspective, the lack of comparison with strong non-LLM or SOTA compiler-based baselines makes it difficult to determine whether the improvements reflect broad effectiveness or mainly internal consistency within the chosen setup.

2. **Reliance on KernelBench runtime measurement.**
The paper uses CUDA event timing with warm-up runs and fixed shapes (lines 669–670). Multiple reviews (LU27DiW5ik note CBiV5Ugi97, c339hUw3cy note vLDg4fdqS2, f4GtuI2blh note OwqbUWVENl) point out that this measurement protocol constitutes a known limitation of KernelBench itself. The recent paper `robust-kbench` [1] discusses how KernelBench can overestimate or mischaracterize runtime improvements and recommends broader evaluation beyond this benchmark. Relying exclusively on KernelBench may therefore not fully establish robustness without additional case-by-case validation or testing on a wider set of kernels, as suggested in both [2] and [3].

Because evaluation methodology is currently an active topic of community discussion, additional clarification on these points would help readers assess the scope and robustness of the paper’s findings.

[1] arXiv, Towards Robust Agentic CUDA Kernel Benchmarking, Verification, and Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14279  
[2] arXiv, Opal: A Modular Framework for Optimizing Performance using Analytics and LLMs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00932  
[3] arXiv, SwizzlePerf: Hardware-Aware LLMs for GPU Kernel Performance Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20258

summary.value:
I'll start with a note about KernelBench. KernelBench is far from a perfect benchmark, but it is the best benchmark that the authors could have been reasonably expected to use at submission. This paper did not propose KernelBench, so it shouldn't be held to its shortcomings. With that said, I do encourage the authors to benchmark their method on updated benchmarks, like robust-kbench, before camera ready. Given how fast this area is evolving, updating the benchmarking to use more recent best practices would greatly increase the value of the paper.

This paper presents STARK, a method for automated GPU kernel optimization. STARK leverages a collaborative multi-agent workflow and several other techniques to manage feedback and balance exploitation vs exploration. STARK is evaluated on KernelBench and outperforms various strong baselines.

All reviewers saw the value and strength of the proposed method. While there were concerns raised, the authors have adequately addressed them.

reviewer_concerns.value:
## Reviewer sbZq

- Evaluation is only on one GPU type. The addition of 3090Ti benchmarking is helpful, but likely doesn't fully address this concern.
- No comparison against ML compilers or modern LLMs. I believe this concern was addressed.
- Lack of analysis of the generated kernels. I believe this was somewhat addressed.

## Reviewer tSQ9

- No feedback from a hardware profiler. I believe this concern was not fully addressed.
- No detailed case study on how the agent discovers strategies that outperform torch.compile. I don't believe this was addressed, but agree with the authors that doing this would be extremely time consuming.

## Reviewer QJHD

 - Robustness to other LLMs. I believe this was addressed.
 - Overhead and runtime needed to create a kernel. I believe this was addressed. This is a metric that is useful to report, but given that the time to create a kernel is an upfront cost paid once, it to some degree doesn't matter.
 - Can STARK outperform human experts. I believe this was addressed.
## Reviewer 5yP2

- The ablation study is insufficient. I believe this was mostly addressed.
- Claude code should be included as a baseline. I believe this was addressed.
- Novelty of the proposed method. I believe this was addressed.
- Manual study of the generated kernels. I believe this was addressed.
- Is the comparison and evaluation fair? I believe this was addressed.

comment.value:
Thank you for your comment. We understand these concerns, and we believe our clarifications below can indeed validate the robustness of our work’s findings.

## LLM choice and Lower-cost LLMs. 

We agree that ablation using other LLMs would provide valuable insights. To this end, we conduct an additional **ablation experiment** where we implement both the baseline agents and our STARK using the **OpenAI GPT-4.1** model, an **economic, lower-cost alternative** to the Claude Sonnet 4 model used in our main experiments. As can be observed from the result table (see in our response to Reviewer sbZq), our framework STARK **maintains significant gains** over baseline agents. 

In addition, with rapid growth of LLMs, **the cost of LLMs decreases fast**. For example, Sonnet 4.5 was released only 4 months after Sonnet 4, and with the new SOTA model, the cost of the original SOTA model can decrease and soon become an economic choice. 

## Baseline Completeness

We appreciate the reviewer for mentioning the baseline completeness, which is in fact one of the most notable **strengths** of our work. 

**In contrast to the cited review notes** where works only compare with torch eager baselines, we compare STARK with **torch compile** baselines, and **we compare with two compilation modes including the highly optimized “max-autotune” mode**. These baselines incorporate highly engineered optimizations developed by domain experts, including operator fusion, kernel scheduling, memory layout transformations, and backend-specific tuning. As such, **they are widely regarded as high-quality implementations** for their target workloads.

## Reliability of KernelBench and Our Experimental Results

We agree that KernelBench is the **de facto benchmark** for measuring LLM agent performance on optimizing GPU kernels. We also appreciate the effort of bringing limitations of KernelBench into attention. 

Importantly, while the problems proposed by [1] are reasonable, they are **irrelevant** to our results and have **no impact on the value and correctness of our results**. Specifically, in the discussions of KernelBench’s limitations, [1] cites two resources: 
- [4] is a **blog post** reporting that about 40 out of the 200 KernelBench (Levels 1-3) problems can be problematic when measuring kernel performances. 
- [5] is a **retracted paper** written by [1]’s authors themselves. 

While we humbly believe these claims should be viewed with caution as they are **informal evidence**, we treat the reliability of KernelBench with **full attention**, and we highlight that 
- Only **20%** of the problems of KernelBench are claimed by [1,4] to be problematic. 
- We focused our evaluation on the **official representative subsets** of KernelBench, which **avoid known limitations** pointed out by the referred review notes and [1], as 
  - The evaluated problems in this work have **minimal overlapping** to the problematic problems identified by [4]. 
  - There are **no** evaluated problems with erroneously small kernel and input tensor size such that the CPU overhead is the dominant factor [1] (these problems are included in the 40 problems identified by [4] and do not overlap with the representative subsets of KernelBench that we used for evaluation).

As a result, the referred notes and works have **minimal impact** on our experimental results. With that being said, **we are more than happy to include more case studies** such as those done in [2,3]. Due to time constraints, we plan to include these in the updated version of our work after the discussion period. 

Lastly, we kindly acknowledge that evaluating **beyond** KernelBench (such as incorporating emerging efforts like robust-kbench) is an important direction for **future work**. While these components are **outside the scope** of our current study, we view them as **natural extensions** and plan to integrate them in subsequent efforts.

Best,

Authors

---

**References.**

[1] arXiv, Towards Robust Agentic CUDA Kernel Benchmarking, Verification, and Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14279.  
[2] arXiv, Opal: A Modular Framework for Optimizing Performance using Analytics and LLMs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00932.  
[3] arXiv, SwizzlePerf: Hardware-Aware LLMs for GPU Kernel Performance Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20258.  
[4] METR. Measuring automated kernel engineering, February 2025. URL https://metr.org/blog/2025-02-14-measuring-automated-kernel-engineering/.   
[5] Robert Tjarko Lange, Aaditya Prasad, Qi Sun, Maxence Faldor, Yujin Tang, and David Ha. The ai cuda engineer: Agentic cuda kernel discovery, optimization and composition. 2025

Dear Reviewer sbZq, 

Thank you for your valuable feedback. We hope our responses address your concerns. 

---

>  ```Evaluated exclusively on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, with no validation on other architectures (e.g., AMD GPUs, edge AI hardware).```

While we would love to test our agent on other hardwares, the testing suite KernelBench currently only supports testing on Nvidia GPUs. To this end, we focus testing our agent on the A100 GPU, the most commonly used high performance GPU. To further validate our agent framework, we conduct extra experiments on the **Nvidia RTX 3090i**, one of the most popular  consumer GPUs. Using the KernelBench Level 2 problems, we observe that our agent **STARK consistently outperforms baseline agents**, generating kernels more than 10x faster. 

Performance Comparisons on Nvidia RTX 3090i. 

| Metric             | Sampling Agent | Reflexion Agent | STARK |
|--------------------|----------|----------|----------|
| fast_1             |    62.5      |     75     |    87.5      |
| STARK speedup over baselines  |    16.5x      |    15.2x      |   -       |
 

> ```Lacks head-to-head testing against state-of-the-art ML/RL-based optimizers (e.g., AlphaTensor, TVM’s Ansor)```

Thank you for this suggestion. 

We would like to clarify that an autonomous GPU optimization agent like STARK is **fundamentally different** to existing ML-based optimizers such as AlphaTensor and Ansor. AlphaTensor discovers algebraic algorithms and Ansor generates TVM schedules, while **STARK is a fully autonomous agent system that starts from raw PyTorch code and directly produces optimized CUDA kernels and fusions** ,a capability outside the scope of these tools. Moreover, STARK requires **no** manual scheduling, IR construction, or search-space design, making it **substantially easier to use**. 

> ```Experiments with Additional Large Language Models (LLMs)``` 

While we focus on instantiating STARK using Anthropic models, we agree that it is helpful to ablate using other SOTA LLMs. To this end, we instantiate baseline agents and STARK on the **OpenAI GPT-4** model, and summarize the key results below. 

Performance Comparisons using OpenAI models. 

| Metric             | Sampling Agent | Reflexion Agent | STARK |
|--------------------|----------|----------|----------|
| fast_1             |    75      |     50     |    87.5      |
| STARK speedup over baselines  |    4.2x      |    5.7x      |   -       |


> ```Provides no analysis of why STARK’s strategies work, no qualitative breakdown of optimization decisions or failure modes.```

We fully agree that a **systematic qualitative analysis** of STARK’s optimization strategies and failure modes is valuable. 

Our **preliminary observation** reveals STARK effectively explores **diverse** optimization paths, **escaping** the local traps where sampling and reflexion agents consistently generate problematic implementations.  

However, conducting such an analysis at a **rigorous level** requires significant effort. In particular, **it involves having kernel experts manually inspect and interpret the full set of CUDA kernels generated across the KernelBench tasks**, analyze their fusion patterns, memory-access decisions, and scheduling strategies, and categorize the underlying optimization behaviors. This process is **highly time-consuming** and cannot be completed within the short rebuttal window. 

We will include a thorough qualitative breakdown (covering representative kernels, decision patterns, and common failure cases) in the final version of this paper. 

Thank you again for this valuable suggestion.

> ```Wall-clock optimization time is not reported.```

Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We record the runtimes of the sampling and reflexion agents, as well as our STARK framework. We summarize the time comparison below, reporting the total time of 30 step optimization for baseline agents and STARK.  

Running Time of Baseline Agents and STARK

|             | Sampling Agent | Reflexion Agent | STARK |
|--------------------|----------|----------|----------|
| Runtime  (mins)          |    154       |     162     |    82.3     | 

Interestingly, despite its more complex orchestration, **STARK’s total runtime is only about half that of the baseline agents**. The **dominant cost** in autonomous kernel optimization is not LLM inference but **kernel compilation and evaluation**, which STARK significantly reduces by generating higher-quality kernels that compile and run more efficiently. In contrast, the baseline agents frequently produce kernels with implementation errors that trigger infinite loops or hit the evaluation timeout, substantially increasing their overall runtime. As a result, STARK’s coordinated design ultimately leads to **faster end-to-end optimization** despite involving more agents.

> ```How would STARK perform if adding another optimization/tuning agent?``` 

We agree that adding additional optimization or tuning agents is a **promising direction**. As with ensemble or mixture-of-experts approaches, incorporating more agents (or even multiple planning/code teams that cross-check each other) could **further improve performance** and reduce the likelihood of errors.

At the same time, introducing more agents increases coordination and communication overhead, which adds complexity beyond the scope of this work. Our goal here is to evaluate the simplest, most direct team design that demonstrates STARK’s **core capabilities**. The framework is modular, and **STARK can be readily extended with additional agents or agent teams in future work**.

Dear Reviewer tSQ9,

Thank you for your thoughtful comments. Please see our response below to your questions. 

---

> ```Though appendix lists some newly generated codes, the paper lacks detailed case study on how these agents end up discovering strategies that beat even torch.compile.```

We fully agree that a **systematic qualitative analysis** of STARK’s optimization strategies is valuable. 

Our **preliminary observation** reveals STARK effectively explores **diverse** optimization paths, **escaping** the local traps where sampling and reflexion agents consistently generate problematic implementations. 

However, conducting such an analysis at a **rigorous level** requires **significant effort**. In particular, **it involves having kernel experts manually inspect and interpret the full set of CUDA kernels generated across the KernelBench tasks**, analyze their fusion patterns, memory-access decisions, and scheduling strategies, and categorize the underlying optimization behaviors. This process is **highly time-consuming** and cannot be completed within the short rebuttal window. 

We will include a thorough qualitative breakdown (covering representative kernels, decision patterns, and common failure cases) in the final version of this paper. 

Thank you again for this valuable suggestion.

> ```How does strategic tree search differ from ABMCTS?``` 

ABMCTS [1] is an MCTS-based search algorithm designed for coding tasks (to pass more tests), while STARK’s search strategy is designed to better optimize GPU kernels. As these two (generating codes that pass tests and optimizing GPU kernel runtime) are **distinct tasks**, they generally **require different search algorithms**. Specifically, we choose the $\epsilon$ -greedy algorithm for STARK, rather than MCTS. 

Our choice is supported by our pilot study comparing representative search policies including Monte-Carlo Tree-Search (MCTS), evolutionary, greedy, and $\epsilon$-greedy policies. In fact, we have compared with UCB-MCTS and **we observe that $\epsilon$-greedy consistently outperforms MCTS for kernel optimization**. We believe this is due to the **nature** of the search space: *kernel optimization often has highly irregular reward landscapes, where runtime improvements are sparse and noisy, and where compilation failures or timeouts create many deceptive branches*. These characteristics violate the assumptions under which AB-MCTS is effective, and likely explain why ε-greedy consistently outperforms UCB-MCTS in our experiments. In this regime, it is very challenging to design a reliable value function for MCTS, while $\epsilon$-greedy’s simpler exploration strategy is more robust and more effective at quickly identifying promising kernel candidates. 

[1] Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search

> ```How does this scale to low resource GPU kernel languages such as Triton?```

We thank the reviewer for raising the question of low-resource kernel languages such as Triton. 

Conceptually, STARK is **language- and backend-agnostic**: it only requires (1) a code-generation interface, (2) a compiler/runtime to execute candidate kernels, and (3) a performance/correctness signal. In this work we focus on CUDA and KernelBench for concreteness and comparability with existing baselines, but the same agent framework can be applied to Triton by swapping the backend tools.

We highlight that changing the target kernel languages primarily affects the **prior knowledge of the base LLM** about a given kernel language, **not** the STARK architecture itself. Since STARK uses iterative compilation, testing, and performance feedback to refine kernels, it does not rely solely on perfect prior familiarity with the language; the feedback loop can correct many initial mistakes. 
**In principle, if an LLM is more fluent in Triton, STARK may benefit from this and achieve even stronger performance**. While fully evaluating this cross-language effect is beyond the scope of our current CUDA-focused study, **extending STARK to Triton is straightforward** and represents an **exciting direction** for future work.

summary.value: This paper introduces STARK, a multi-agent LLM framework for GPU kernel optimization. STARK adopts a collaborative multi-agent workflow with specialized planner, coder, and debugger agents operating at different temperatures, and grounded instruction and dynamic context windows to leverage historical context. The better search algorithm with tree memory uses an adapted ε-greedy policy to balance exploration and exploitation. The proposed approach outperforms sampling agents and reflexion agents.

comment.value:
> ```Why are siblings (S(i)) are expected to have similarities? Some evidence indicating its importance in Wdebug and Wcode would be useful.```

Thank you for this constructive question. Siblings S(i) are expected to share similarities because, by construction, they all descend from the same parent node and therefore represent closely related kernel variants obtained through small, localized transformations. Consequently, nodes in S(i) typically share the same structural scaffolds—such as the loop structure, memory layout, or fusion pattern—as their parent, with only targeted modifications applied by the planning or coding agent. This leads to strong correlations in both their implementation error modes and their micro-optimization patterns.

To validate that siblings are indeed helpful, we **conduct an extra ablation study on the effect of dynamic context window** (which controls **how many siblings** an agent sees). As shown in the following table, dynamic context window demonstrates notable value by increasing both the fast_1 rate and speedup over the baseline agents (from ~10x to 16x). 
 
Performance of STARK with Different Sizes of Dynamic Context Window

 | Metric             | No Dynamic Context Window | STARK | 
|--------------------|----------|----------|
| fast_1             |   75 |  87.5  |   
| STARK speedup over the reflexion agent baselines  |    10.3x   |  16x  |    

> ```No hardware profiler feedback integration. Since hardware feedback can give lot more insight to planning agent. How does hardware feedback improve the overall framework output further? ```

Thank you for this insightful comment. We experimented with explicitly providing the hardware type (e.g., exact GPU model) in STARK’s prompts, but observe **no** measurable performance gains. **This aligns with observations reported in KernelBench**, where LLM agents also show limited ability to translate raw hardware descriptions into actionable low-level optimizations.
We believe this reflects a broader limitation of current LLMs: they do not reliably leverage parametric knowledge about GPU microarchitectures to guide kernel generation. 

**Addressing this likely requires integrating structured hardware information through more advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques.** While developing such a system is an exciting direction, it is an orthogonal research project and thus outside the scope of the current work.

Dear Reviewer QjHD,

We appreciate your constructive feedback. Please see our response below. 

---

> ```it’d help to show robustness to other base LLMs and to ablate prompt dependencies.``` 

Thank you for this suggestion. Due to time and budget constraints, we use KernelBench level 2 problems with medium difficulty for our ablation studies. We first follow your advice to conduct ablation studies using OpenAI models (GPT 4.1). We observe that our framework STARK **maintains significant gains** over baseline agents. 

Performance Comparisons using OpenAI models. 

| Metric             | Sampling Agent | Reflexion Agent | STARK |
|--------------------|----------|----------|----------|
| fast_1             |    75      |     50     |    87.5      |
| STARK speedup over agent baselines  |    4.2x      |    5.7x      |   -       |


In addition, we ablated the effect of system prompt. In the original experiments for STARK, we used the same system prompt used by KernelBench. To ablate its robustness to prompts, we ask GPT-5.1 to generate two different yet semantically similar alternatives to the KernelBench system prompt (we include the generated alternatives in Figure 6 and 7 in Appendix).  We observe that STARK’s performance is **robust to varying system prompts**. 

Performance Comparisons with Varying System Prompts. 

| Metric             | STARK (Original) | STARK (Prompt V1) | STARK (Prompt V2) |
|--------------------|----------|----------|----------|
| fast_1             |    87.5      |     87.5     |    87.5      |
| STARK speedup over the reflexion agent baselines  |    16x      |    14.5x     |   17.1x  |

> ```STARK outperforms baseline agent kernels, but it's unknown its kernels' performance against expert written kernels```

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding comparisons against expert-written kernels. 

While manually crafted kernels can, in isolated cases, offer additional performance gains, **they are often not available for the diverse set of operators and models covered in KernelBench**, and producing them requires significant engineering effort. Our goal is to evaluate STARK in realistic scenarios where users rely on existing compiler stacks rather than handcrafted kernels.  

In this work, following the setup of KernelBench, **we evaluate STARK against the strongest available practical baselines**: torch.compile–generated kernels, which represent the **state-of-the-art in production-grade compiler optimizations**. In particular, while KernelBench only compares to the ‘default’ mode of compilation, **we extensively compare with three compilation modes including the highly optimized “max-autotune” mode**. These baselines incorporate highly engineered optimizations developed by domain experts, including operator fusion, kernel scheduling, memory layout transformations, and backend-specific tuning. As such, **they are widely regarded as high-quality implementations** for their target workloads.

> ```Sensitivity to  Hyperparameters.```  

Conceptually, these hyperparameters mostly govern the efficiency and breadth of the search rather than introducing qualitatively different behaviors. While the optimal values are problem-dependent, STARK’s overall performance is **robust to their choices**. In particular, we choose their values in our pilot study using two problems not in the evaluation sets, and **we then fix their values for all evaluation problems of KernelBench**, showing STARK’s **insensitivity** to these hyperparameters.

summary.value: This paper introduces STARK, an LLM-based agentic framework for automated GPU kernel optimization, addressing the inefficiency of existing methods (manual optimization, automated compilers, single-agent LLMs) in navigating irregular kernel design spaces. STARK’s core innovations include: a collaborative multi-agent workflow (plan/code/debug agents with role-specific temperatures), grounded instruction (anchoring optimization plans to code spans) and dynamic context windows (agent-specific historical feedback), and strategic search (tree memory with adapted ε-greedy policy to balance exploration/exploitation). Evaluated on KernelBench (3 difficulty levels), STARK outperforms baselines (Sampling/Reflexion agents, Torch Eager/Compile) by achieving 100% success rate across levels, up to 16× speedup over Reflexion, and resolving challenging Level 3 tasks where baselines fail. It demonstrates that multi-agent collaboration and feedback-driven search unlock LLMs’ potential for scalable, fully automated GPU kernel optimization.

strengths.value:
1. Innovative multi-agent framework decomposes tasks into planning, coding, debugging roles with tailored parameters. Combined with grounded instructions and dynamic context, it bridges the planning-implementation gap, achieving 100% success rate across all KernelBench levels.
2. Strategic search with tree memory uses an adapted ε-greedy policy to avoid redundancy and local optima, gaining up to 16× speedup over baselines. Ablation studies confirm gains from its combination with multi-agent workflow.
3. Evaluated on multi-difficulty KernelBench, compared with multiple baselines, and assessed via metrics like success rate. It fully verifies performance and provides a clear benchmark for similar research.

weaknesses.value:
1. Evaluated exclusively on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, with no validation on other architectures (e.g., AMD GPUs, edge AI hardware).
2. Lacks head-to-head testing against state-of-the-art ML/RL-based optimizers (e.g., AlphaTensor, TVM’s Ansor) and modern LLMs (e.g., GPT-4, DeepSeek-R1).
3. Provides no analysis of why STARK’s strategies (e.g., grounded instruction) work, no qualitative breakdown of optimization decisions or failure modes.

summary.value: The paper proposes STARK, a multi-agent LLM framework for GPU-kernel optimization. It splits work into plan / code / debug agents, coordinates them with grounded instructions. On KernelBench, STARK markedly outperforms baseline agents in both success rate and runtime speed.

strengths.value:
1. The plan/code/debug split is well-motivated and practical.
2. The grounded instruction concretize edits and tighten plan–implementation alignment.
3. The empirical results demonstrates kernels generated by STARK having consistent improvement in Fast1, success rate, and speed, as well as compile and correct rate.

weaknesses.value:
1. All agents use Claude Sonnet 4; it’d help to show robustness to other base LLMs and to ablate prompt dependencies.
2. The multi-agent workflow + search adds overhead. Wall-clock optimization time (not just kernel runtime) is not reported.
3. STARK outperforms baseline agent kernels, but it's unknown its kernels' performance against expert written kernels.
4. (misc) Typos such as "Kernel Execuation Result" and "Due to space constrain"

questions.value:
1. How would STARK perform if adding another optimization/tuning agent?
2. How sensitive are results to ε, root throttling cap, dead-branch threshold, and context-window size?

summary.value: STARK proposes multi agent framework for iterative refinement GPU kernels for performance optimization. STARK consists of 3 different agents namely for planning, coding, and debugging implemented using the same LLM claude-4-sonnet but distinct sampling parameter e.g., temperature. Planning agents prepares a plan to explore optimization strategies. Coder agents works on top of planning agent output to produce code that best aligns with strategies produced by the planning agent. Debugging agent repairs the code based on execution and hardware feedback. STARK leverages grounded instructions to guide planning/coding agent to suggest/generate edits in specific parts of the code as desired. Furthermore, dynamic context window is leveraged to feed relevant but contrastive in-context learning samples to all planning, coding, and debug agents. STARK populates dynamic context window by maintaining a persistent tree of prior attempts (generated code) to guide future planning/coding attempts to produce better kernels. STARK compares against torch eager & compile mode and reflexion agent-based implementation. STARK achieves 100% success rate across first 3 levels of kernelbench benchmark and outperforms baseline run time by up to 3x.

strengths.value:
- Multi agent realization of one of the toughest coding tasks of GPU kernel generation.
- Clear division of work across 3 different agents and their seamless integration to produce better kernel.
- Tree of prior attempts that helps to systematically identify good candidates for iterative refinement instead of blind refinement. 
- grounded instructions and dynamic context windows that help carefully plan and target code edits.

weaknesses.value:
- No hardware profiler feedback integration. Since hardware feedback can give lot more insight to planning agent.
- Though appendix lists some newly generated codes, the paper lacks detailed case study on how these agents end up discovering strategies that beat even torch.compile.

questions.value:
- How does this scale to low resource GPU kernel languages such as Triton?
- How does strategic tree search differ from ABMCTS? What is the comparison in performance w.r.t. ABMCTS?
- Why are siblings (S(i)) are expected to have similarities? Some evidence indicating its importance in Wdebug and Wcode would be useful.
- How does hardware feedback improve the overall framework output further?

comment.value:
>  ```Are all baselines using the same computing resources (e.g., same API costs)?```

We understand your concern, and we conduct experiments where the baseline agents use **4 times more attempts** than STARK, making them equal in API costs. 

*Performance of Baseline Agents with Extra Budgets* 

| Metric                         | Sampling Agent | Sampling Agent (4x) | Reflexion Agent | Reflexion Agent (4x) | STARK |
|--------------------------------|----------------|----------------------|------------------|------------------------|--------|
| fast_1                         | 37.5           | 37.5                 | 62.5             | 62.5                   | 87.5   |
| STARK speedup over baselines   | 2.35x          | 2.31x                | 16x              | 16x                    | -      |


We observe that, even with 4 times the attempts, **the baseline agents cannot effectively enhance their performance** due to **severely diminishing return**. In particular, the reflexion agent keeps stuck in similar local optimums and struggles to improve while the sampling agent’s efficiency in generating strong kernels is very low so that the fast_1 rates remain unchanged, and the fastest generated kernels have minimal speed improvement. 

These results exactly demonstrate the challenge of GPU kernel optimization, and **advanced agentic features such as the ones proposed by STARK are necessary for effectively finding better GPU kernels with more budgets**. 

> ```How novel is the strategic search with tree memory? ... How does this work compare against "Astra: A Multi-Agent System for GPU Kernel Performance Optimization" in terms of the proposed method?```


We note that strategic search with tree memory is one of the most classic ideas for AI. However, **novelties lie in the exact instantiation of strategic search for a given problem, in our case, the GPU kernel optimization**. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to **successfully apply strategic search with LLM agent for autonomous GPU kernel optimization**. For example, the referred work [1] chooses an iterative optimization approach. 

**Comparison with [1].** We appreciate the reviewer for pointing us to the concurrent work Astra [1]. We will include this work into our related work discussion. However, our STARK framework is very different from [1] for two main reasons. 

**Optimization Scope and Objective.** [1] focuses on continual optimization of existing SGLang CUDA implementations while STARK generates CUDA kernels for raw Pytorch code. They are very different application scenarios and thus orthogonal to each other. 

**Algorithm Difference.** More importantly, while both [1] and STARK have multi-agent component (STARK has an additional debugging agent), STARK has many **additional algorithmic features** including 
- *Strategic Search with adaptations for GPU optimization* including root throttling, dead-thread threshold and leaf-biased exploration 
- *Grounded Instruction*
- *Dynamic Context Window*

All of which are proven to be effective for the optimization setting of STARK.

> **Comparison with Claude Code** 

Thank you for this suggestion. 

We kindly note that Claude Code is designed as a coding assistant that **completes human-assigned tasks** within a potential human-in-the-loop paradigm. In contrast, STARK is designed to **optimize** code pieces (GPU kernels). Thus, Claude Code and STARK have **different goals and objectives**.  Moreover, Claude Code has **no access** to the profiling tools of STARK. 

**Experiment Setup.** To fairly compare STARK with Claude Code with STARK, **we provide the profiling tool as a script that can be called by Claude Code**, and thus the evaluation output can be observed by Claude Code. We ask Claude Code to generate CUDA kernels as code files and then use the given profiling script to evaluate the generated kernels. We give Claude Code **full freedom** to check all its historical attempts and continue optimization. Before the optimization starts, we tell Claude Code that you have 30 attempts in total (the same number of attempts used by STARK). 

**Observations.** We report the results in the following table. Notably, Claude Code demonstrates unsatisfactory performance, barely outperforming the sampling agent. Based on our observation of its execution, we believe this is caused by its lack of effective strategic search capability and its ineffective management of context windows for GPU optimization (when given full freedom, Claude Code demonstrates a close-to-random search process), **further establishing the value of STARK**.
